{{Short description|Mathematical model in optimal trade execution}}

The '''Almgren–Chriss model''' is a mathematical model in [[mathematical finance]] for the [[optimal execution]] of large [[portfolio (finance)|portfolio]] transactions. Developed by [[Robert Almgren]] and [[Neil Chriss]] in a series of working papers in 1999 and published in 2000, the model frames the liquidation of a large position over a fixed time horizon as a [[mean-variance]] trade-off between [[market impact]] costs (incurred by trading too quickly) and [[volatility|timing risk]] (incurred by trading too slowly).<ref name="AC2000">{{cite journal |last1=Almgren |first1=Robert |last2=Chriss |first2=Neil |year=2001 |title=Optimal execution of portfolio transactions |journal=Journal of Risk |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=5–39 |doi=10.21314/JOR.2001.041}}</ref><ref name="Cartea2015">{{cite book |last1=Cartea |first1=Álvaro |last2=Jaimungal |first2=Sebastian |last3=Penalva |first3=José |title=Algorithmic and High-Frequency Trading |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2015 |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-1-107-09114-6}}</ref> It is one of the foundational results in the modern theory of [[algorithmic trading]] and remains widely used in institutional [[execution algorithm]]s.<ref name="Cartea2015" /><ref name="GatheralSchied" />

==Background==
The optimal execution problem arises when a [[trader (finance)|trader]] must buy or sell a quantity of an asset large enough that the act of trading itself affects the asset's price. Trading the entire position immediately ("market order") moves the price adversely and produces a poor average execution price; spreading the trade over a long interval reduces this price impact but exposes the trader to [[market risk|price risk]] from independent market movements over the execution window.<ref name="Cartea2015" /><ref name="GatheralSchied">{{cite book |last1=Gatheral |first1=Jim |last2=Schied |first2=Alexander |year=2013 |chapter=Dynamical models of market impact and algorithms for order execution |title=Handbook on Systemic Risk |editor1-last=Fouque |editor1-first=Jean-Pierre |editor2-last=Langsam |editor2-first=Joseph A. |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=579–602 |isbn=978-1-107-02343-7}}</ref>

The problem was first studied formally by [[Dimitris Bertsimas|Bertsimas]] and [[Andrew Lo|Lo]] in 1998, who derived an optimal trajectory under risk-neutral preferences and a linear permanent impact.<ref name="BertsimasLo">{{cite journal |last1=Bertsimas |first1=Dimitris |last2=Lo |first2=Andrew W. |year=1998 |title=Optimal control of execution costs |journal=Journal of Financial Markets |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–50 |doi=10.1016/S1386-4181(97)00012-8}}</ref> Almgren and Chriss extended this framework to risk-averse traders by introducing a mean–variance objective and an explicit distinction between permanent and temporary impact, producing closed-form optimal trajectories that depend on the trader's risk aversion.<ref name="AC2000" /><ref name="LokkaXu">{{cite arXiv |last1=Løkka |first1=Arne |last2=Xu |first2=Junwei |year=2020 |title=Optimal liquidation trajectories for the Almgren–Chriss model with Lévy processes |eprint=2002.03376 |class=q-fin.MF}}</ref>

==Model formulation==
A trader holds <math>X</math> shares of a single asset and must liquidate the position by a deadline <math>T</math>. Time is divided into <math>N</math> intervals of length <math>\tau = T/N</math>, and the trader chooses a sequence of holdings <math>x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N</math>, with <math>x_0 = X</math> and <math>x_N = 0</math>. The number of shares sold in interval <math>k</math> is <math>n_k = x_{k-1} - x_k</math>, and the corresponding selling rate is <math>v_k = n_k / \tau</math>.<ref name="AC2000" /><ref name="Cartea2015" />

The model assumes that the asset's unaffected price follows an [[arithmetic Brownian motion]],

:<math>S_k = S_{k-1} + \sigma \sqrt{\tau} \, \xi_k - \tau \, g(v_k),</math>

where <math>\sigma</math> is the price volatility, the <math>\xi_k</math> are independent standard [[normal distribution|normal]] shocks, and <math>g(v_k)</math> is the '''permanent market impact''' function representing the lasting effect of the trade on the equilibrium price. In addition, each trade is executed at a price that differs from the prevailing price by a '''temporary market impact''' <math>h(v_k)</math>, reflecting the immediate liquidity cost that does not persist:<ref name="AC2000" /><ref name="Cartea2015" />

:<math>\tilde{S}_k = S_{k-1} - h(v_k).</math>

In the original Almgren–Chriss paper, both impact functions are taken to be linear in the trading rate: <math>g(v) = \gamma v</math> and <math>h(v) = \eta v</math>, with <math>\gamma, \eta > 0</math>.<ref name="AC2000" />

The total expected cost of the execution (the [[implementation shortfall]]) and its variance can then be expressed in closed form as functions of the holdings trajectory <math>\{x_k\}</math>. The trader minimises

:<math>\mathbb{E}[C] + \lambda \, \mathrm{Var}[C],</math>

where <math>C</math> is the total transaction cost and <math>\lambda \geq 0</math> is a [[risk aversion]] parameter.<ref name="AC2000" />

==Optimal trajectory==
For linear impact functions, the optimal liquidation trajectory has the closed form

:<math>x_k = X \, \frac{\sinh\bigl(\kappa (T - t_k)\bigr)}{\sinh(\kappa T)},</math>

where <math>\kappa</math> is a constant determined by the impact and risk-aversion parameters,

:<math>\kappa = \frac{1}{\tau}\,\mathrm{arccosh}\!\left(\frac{\tau^2}{2}\,\tilde{\kappa}^2 + 1\right), \qquad \tilde{\kappa}^2 = \frac{\lambda \sigma^2}{\eta - \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma\tau}.</math>

The trajectory is a [[hyperbolic functions|hyperbolic]] sine curve that interpolates between two limiting cases:<ref name="AC2000" /><ref name="Cartea2015" />

* When <math>\lambda = 0</math> (the risk-neutral case), the optimal trajectory is linear in time, recovering the [[time-weighted average price]] (TWAP) execution schedule.<ref name="AC2000" />
* As <math>\lambda \to \infty</math>, the trader becomes infinitely averse to timing risk and the optimal trajectory degenerates to immediate liquidation at <math>t = 0</math>.<ref name="AC2000" />

In intermediate cases, the more risk-averse the trader, the more front-loaded the execution schedule: a larger fraction of the position is liquidated near the start of the interval to reduce the variance of the realised cost.<ref name="Cartea2015" /><ref name="GatheralSchied" />

==Extensions==
The original model has been extended in several directions:

* '''Non-linear impact functions.''' Almgren generalised the model in 2003 to allow non-linear (typically power-law) temporary impact, motivated by empirical observations that price concession grows sub-linearly in trade size.<ref name="Almgren2003">{{cite journal |last=Almgren |first=Robert |year=2003 |title=Optimal execution with nonlinear impact functions and trading-enhanced risk |journal=Applied Mathematical Finance |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=1–18 |doi=10.1080/135048602100056}}</ref>
* '''Continuous-time and stochastic-control formulations.''' Continuous-time versions of the model have been developed using [[Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation|Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman]] methods, allowing for dynamic re-optimisation and richer price dynamics.<ref name="GatheralSchied" /><ref name="LokkaXu" />
* '''Volume-dependent extensions.''' Kato introduced an explicit trading-volume process into the framework and showed that, in the risk-neutral limit, the optimal execution coincides with a [[volume-weighted average price|VWAP]]-tracking strategy.<ref name="Kato">{{cite journal |last=Kato |first=Takashi |year=2015 |title=VWAP execution as an optimal strategy |journal=JSIAM Letters |volume=7 |pages=33–36 |doi=10.14495/jsiaml.7.33|arxiv=1408.6118 }}</ref>
* '''Adaptive strategies.''' Almgren and Lorenz showed that, because the variance objective is dynamically inconsistent, adaptive strategies that re-optimise as new price information arrives improve on the static Almgren–Chriss schedule.<ref name="AlmgrenLorenz">{{cite journal |last1=Almgren |first1=Robert |last2=Lorenz |first2=Julian |year=2007 |title=Adaptive arrival price |journal=Algorithmic Trading III: Precision, Control, Execution |publisher=Institutional Investor}}</ref>

==Applications==
The Almgren–Chriss framework underlies a large class of institutional execution algorithms, including implementation-shortfall and arrival-price strategies offered by major [[broker-dealer]]s and execution venues.<ref name="Cartea2015" /><ref name="GatheralSchied" />
